title: Warmly vs Knock AI vs Storylane RepX: 2026 Comparison
summary: Warmly vs Knock AI compared with a neutral rubric: real 2026 pricing, reviews, the HubSpot acquisition impact, and where Storylane RepX fits.
body_markdown:
Most "Warmly vs Knock AI" pages are written by Warmly or Knock AI, so of course each one crowns itself. Here is my actual thesis: this is not a "which tool is better" question, it is a "which motion fits your team" question, and in 2026 the single biggest variable is not features at all, it is that Warmly now lives inside HubSpot. I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and I will be upfront that we build a competing category (RepX), so I will show my scoring math and tell you plainly where we do not fit.


> **Definition:** A *website visitor engagement platform* identifies who is on your site (often anonymously), scores their intent, and engages them in real time through chat, outbound, or routing, so high-intent traffic becomes pipeline instead of a bounce.


If you take one thing from this comparison of Warmly vs Knock AI, take this: Warmly is signal-first (de-anonymize, score, then nurture), Knock AI is conversation-first (engage in the moment across channels), and the right pick depends on whether your gap is *data* or *dialogue* .


## Warmly vs Knock AI at a glance (TL;DR)


Here is the short version before the detail, because the searcher for this query is in decision mode, not learning mode.


- **Warmly** is a mature, signal-first platform: strong de-anonymization, intent scoring, and orchestration, now owned by HubSpot as of 2026.
- **Knock AI** is an early-stage, conversation-first platform: multi-channel AI engagement across web chat, Slack, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp, with a thinner third-party track record.
- **Pricing** favors Knock AI as a flat monthly line item; Warmly is cheaper to *start* (free plan) but its AI-chat-capable tiers climb into enterprise range.
- **Reviews** favor Warmly on volume and independent validation; Knock AI is materially under-reviewed, which is a real risk, not a rounding error.
- **The wildcard** is the HubSpot acquisition, which reshapes Warmly's roadmap, pricing leverage, and lock-in profile in ways no competitor page will tell you.


One-line verdict: pick Warmly if you live in HubSpot and want proven signal infrastructure; pick Knock AI if conversation and channel breadth matter more than pedigree; and read the RepX disclosure section if your real problem is demos, not visitor ID.


## Quick-reference comparison table


This is the single most-expected asset for the query, so here it is up front, with Storylane RepX included for the demo-led reader.


Capability Warmly Knock AI Storylane RepX


Core model Signal-first: de-anonymize, score, nurture Conversation-first: engage in the moment Demo-first: AI agent that runs interactive demos


Visitor de-anonymization Yes, core strength (~65% companies, ~15% contacts) Yes, via Knock Reveal No, not a visitor-ID tool


Real-time intent scoring Yes, mature Yes, via Knock Intent Engagement-signal based, demo-centric


Engagement channels Web chat, orchestrated outbound, HubSpot Web chat, Slack, LinkedIn, WhatsApp Interactive demos, guided tours, in-demo chat


AI qualification/chat Yes Yes, via Knock Agent Yes, demo-native AI agent


CRM integrations Native HubSpot (post-acquisition), others HubSpot and common CRMs HubSpot, Salesforce, common CRMs

Starting price Free, then modular paid tiers ~$1,000/mo Foundation Not publicly listed


Best for HubSpot-standardized, signal-led GTM teams Conversation-led, multi-channel teams Demo-led buying experiences


Treat the vendor-supplied numbers above as claims to verify, not settled fact. The pricing and identification-rate rows in particular move, which is exactly why the sections below carry dates and attributions.


Read the table top to bottom and it tells one story: Warmly and Knock AI are competing for the same "convert anonymous traffic" job from opposite directions, while RepX is solving an adjacent problem entirely. If your eye keeps landing on the RepX column, that is a hint your bottleneck is the demo, not visitor identification, and the rest of this piece will help you confirm it.


## What is Warmly? (2026 status)


Warmly is the incumbent of this pairing and the more established product. Founded in 2020 and having raised roughly $17M (Felicis Series A plus an RTP Global extension), it built its reputation on person-level de-anonymization plus signal-based orchestration.


The model is signal-first. Warmly reveals the companies and, less often, the individual contacts browsing your site, scores their intent, and then routes or nurtures them, claiming to reveal roughly 65% of companies and 15% of contacts (Warmly, 2026).


The headline 2026 fact is ownership. Warmly was acquired by HubSpot in 2026, which turns a best-of-breed point tool into part of a platform, with everything that implies for roadmap and pricing leverage. I devote a full section to what that acquisition actually changes, because every competitor comparison conveniently skips it.


> **Bottom line on Warmly:** deep, proven de-anonymization and a genuine free entry point, now paired with native HubSpot alignment, offset by real post-acquisition uncertainty about roadmap and packaging.


## What is Knock AI? (2026 status)


Knock AI is the challenger, and it competes on conversation rather than pedigree. It is early-stage, only a couple of years old, with correspondingly thin third-party benchmarking, so you are betting more on trajectory than on track record.


Its architecture splits into three named pieces: Knock Reveal for visitor identification, Knock Intent for scoring, and Knock Agent for the AI conversation layer. The differentiator it leans on is channel breadth, engaging prospects across web chat, Slack, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp rather than the website alone.


Knock AI also markets aggressive performance figures, such as reply rates as high as 86% and meaningfully faster click-to-opportunity, but these are the vendor's own numbers with no independent validation, so I would treat them as marketing until a third party confirms them. If you are evaluating challengers like this, it is worth also scanning the broader field of[best AI SDR tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/top-ai-sdr-tools) before committing, since the category moves fast.


- **Strength:** true multi-channel engagement, not just on-site chat.
- **Strength:** simple, flat monthly pricing that is easy to budget.
- **Watch item:** minimal independent reviews and a short operating history.


## Feature-by-feature comparison


This is the heart of the query, so I score each capability and end every subsection with a plain verdict rather than a hedge. I have organized it around the five capabilities buyers actually shortlist on, not the two dozen a vendor deck lists to look thorough.


Read the verdicts as directional, not absolute, because the right answer flips depending on whether your gap is data or dialogue. Where the two tools genuinely tie, I say so instead of inventing a difference to fill the row.


Each subsection follows the same rhythm: what the capability is, how the two vendors actually differ on it, and a one-line verdict you can act on. I weight proven behavior over roadmap promises throughout, because in this category the gap between a demo and production is where most buyer regret lives.


### Visitor identification / de-anonymization


Both tools de-anonymize traffic, but Warmly has the longer track record and the more-cited coverage numbers, while Knock Reveal is newer and less independently benchmarked. The real evaluation question is not "does it identify visitors" but "how accurately does it separate real prospects from noise."


That distinction matters more than vendors admit, because a buyer we spoke with described exactly this failure mode in their own stack.


> "I also get there might be for example somebody searching for job. Right. And coming on any page might be exploring more about the product. But they are not a prospect." - \[Founding team member, growth-stage software\]


So when you trial either tool, test how well it filters job seekers, internal users, and casual browsers out of your "high-intent" list. **Verdict:** Warmly wins on maturity and disclosed coverage; Knock AI is credible but unproven, so demand a live accuracy test before you believe either number.


### Real-time intent scoring & signals


Warmly's intent scoring is mature and tightly linked to its orchestration, which is its whole reason for existing. Knock Intent covers the same ground conceptually but has less public evidence of accuracy at scale.


The value of scoring is only realized if it feeds a motion, which is why intent data belongs inside a broader plan rather than sitting in a dashboard. If you are wiring either tool into demand gen, it pays to first[build an ABM funnel](https://www.storylane.io/blog/perfect-abm-funnel) so the scores route to the right play instead of a generic alert.


The buyers we hear from rarely struggle to *collect* signals; they struggle to act on them without looping in ops. A scoring engine that fires an alert nobody can route is worse than no score at all, because it manufactures guilt instead of pipeline.


So the question to ask each vendor is concrete: when this tool scores an account hot, what happens in the next five minutes, and can a marketer change that play without engineering. **Verdict:** roughly even on concept, with Warmly ahead on proven signal depth and Knock AI ahead on packaging simplicity.


### Engagement channels & AI chat/qualification


This is where the two philosophies diverge most sharply. Warmly concentrates engagement on the website and orchestrated follow-up, whereas Knock AI spreads it across web chat, Slack, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp.


If your buyers convert in a live on-site moment, channel breadth is noise; if they scatter across surfaces, it is the point. Teams building a modern buying experience often pair either tool with[digital sales room software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/digital-sales-room-software) so the conversation has somewhere substantive to land.


The trap is buying channels you will not staff. Every extra surface, Slack, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, is another place a prospect can start a conversation your team has to answer quickly, and an unanswered AI-initiated chat does more damage than never opening one.


Be honest about where your buyers actually reply before you pay for reach you cannot cover. A founding-team buyer we spoke with framed the goal as simply wanting to initiate more chats and capture more emails from existing traffic, which is a volume problem, not a channel-count problem. **Verdict:** Knock AI wins on channel breadth; Warmly wins on depth of the on-site and HubSpot-connected motion.


### Outbound orchestration & follow-up


Orchestration is where the "signal-first" label earns its keep, and it is Warmly's stronger suit: identify, score, then trigger the right outbound or routing automatically. Knock AI's outbound is real but younger, leaning on its conversational agent to carry follow-up across channels.


The buyer problem underneath this is that most teams are holding follow-up together with brittle glue, and one marketing manager described theirs bluntly.


> "We use Zapier set up to do a bunch of things right now with lead flow stuff... we would need to talk to our ops people about how this might work." - \[Marketing Manager, B2B SaaS\]


When a stack depends on ops to change a Zap, every "orchestration" claim should be tested against how easily *your* team can edit a play without engineering. Automation that only the person who built it can maintain is a liability dressed up as a feature.


Ask for a live edit during the demo: change a routing rule in front of you, and watch who has to touch it. **Verdict:** Warmly for structured, signal-triggered orchestration; Knock AI for conversation-led follow-up across more surfaces.


### CRM & integrations (incl. the HubSpot-native angle post-acquisition)


Post-acquisition, Warmly's HubSpot integration stops being "an integration" and starts being "native," which is a genuine advantage if HubSpot is your system of record. Knock AI connects to HubSpot and common CRMs too, but as a partner rather than an owner.


The honest complication is that not every team is standardized on HubSpot, and a buyer captured that tension exactly.


> "It would have been really good if the decision was made to use HubSpot as the company wide CRM. But we are where we are." - \[Digital Marketing Director, B2B SaaS\]


If your CRM reality is messy, weigh how each tool creates and updates records, because that plumbing is where deals quietly break. The specific setting to interrogate is whether the tool can update existing leads and contacts only, or whether it insists on creating its own records and forking your data.


For a non-HubSpot team, Warmly's new native advantage is largely irrelevant, and the neutral parity with Knock AI reasserts itself. **Verdict:** Warmly wins decisively for HubSpot-standardized teams; the advantage shrinks fast if you run a mixed or non-HubSpot stack.


## Warmly vs Knock AI pricing compared (real numbers)


Pricing is the section every competitor blurs, so here it is with dates and the caveat that both vendors gate their full tiers behind a demo. Figures are current as of 2026 and should be re-verified before you sign.


Plan level Warmly Knock AI


Free Yes, up to 500 visitors/mo No published free plan


Entry paid Modular paid tiers, roughly $10K/yr floor ~$1,000/mo (Pipeline Foundation)


Mid AI-chat-capable tiers climbing toward ~$30K/yr ~$2,000/mo (Acceleration)


Top Full GTM, custom/quote Custom Enterprise


Two things deserve emphasis. Warmly's pricing is modular and largely quote-based, so a single "entry price" is misleading; it is cheapest to *start* on the free plan, but its AI-chat-capable tier can land near $30K/yr (Warmly, 2026). Knock AI is a cleaner flat line item and recently raised its floor from roughly $700 to $1,000/mo, which tells you the price is moving upward, not settling.


The buyer takeaway is simple: "cheaper" depends entirely on the tier you actually need. Do not compare Knock AI's entry price against Warmly's free plan and call it a match, because the AI-chat capability you probably want sits much higher on Warmly's ladder.


Because both vendors gate full tiers behind a demo, insist on a written quote for the exact tier and visitor volume you will run, dated, before you compare. A range with no date is how a "cheaper" tool becomes a surprise renewal, and both of these vendors have already moved their numbers this year.


## What real users say (reviews)


Review depth is a differentiator here because it is lopsided, and no competitor page admits how lopsided. Warmly carries meaningful independent validation, rated roughly 4.6 out of 5 across about 201 reviews (G2, 2026).


Knock AI, by contrast, has very few third-party reviews so far, which is exactly what you would expect from an early-stage product but is still a risk you are underwriting. Thin review volume means you are relying on the vendor's narrative and your own trial rather than a body of peer evidence.


My advice: weight Warmly's reviews as real signal, and for Knock AI, insist on live references from teams that match your size and motion. An under-reviewed tool is not disqualified, but it does shift the burden of proof onto your own hands-on evaluation.


Read the negative reviews first, not the five-star ones, because the one-and-two-star reviews tell you where a tool breaks in production. For Knock AI, the absence of that volume is itself the finding: you cannot pattern-match failure modes that no one has written up yet, so plan a longer, more skeptical evaluation.


## Implementation & time-to-value


Neither tool is truly "plug and play," and the honest benchmark is weeks of configuration, not days, once you account for routing, playbooks, and CRM sync. The friction is rarely the software itself; it is the record-creation logic and the automation debt already in your stack.


A digital marketing buyer described the kind of integration mess that turns a two-week rollout into a two-month one.


> "We have a ton of contact information that went into the system before the integration happened. And because of the way the integration has happened it means that we've got two, two CRM systems where only 14%. 14% Of our records are actually synced properly. So it's a bit of a headache right." - \[Digital Marketing Director, B2B SaaS\]


Use this checklist before you commit to either platform:


1. Map exactly how records get created and updated, and whether the tool can update existing leads only.
2. Inventory the Zaps and automations the new tool will replace or collide with.
3. Confirm who owns setup changes, because dependence on an ops queue is where time-to-value dies.
4. Book a hand-off test, then[run a tighter discovery call](https://www.storylane.io/blog/discovery-call-agenda) against the leads the tool actually surfaces.


**Verdict:** budget weeks for either, and judge the vendor on how much of that configuration they own versus how much they leave to your ops team.


## Where Storylane RepX fits


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane builds RepX, an AI sales agent that lives inside interactive demos rather than in a website-visitor-ID layer, so I want to be precise about the mechanism instead of pitching.


RepX works when the buying decision hinges on *seeing the product* , not on being identified in the first ten seconds on a pricing page. The agent runs a guided interactive demo, answers questions in-context, and qualifies based on how someone engages with the product itself, which is a different signal than "which company is on my site."


That means RepX does **not** replace Warmly or Knock AI for anonymous visitor de-anonymization; if your core gap is "I can see company interest but only capture form-fills," a visitor-ID tool is the right category, not us. A marketing ops buyer framed that exact gap.


> "Right now we are having data from Storylane, but when they fill in the form. But we also see some interest from companies. They don't fill form but they like view the profile, etc. And we want to leverage that and we want to integrate that Data to our CRM." - \[Marketing Operations Analyst, B2B SaaS\]


So the honest boundary is this: use Warmly or Knock AI to identify and engage anonymous traffic, and use RepX when the moment that matters is the demo. They can coexist, and pretending otherwise would be the vendor-pitch move this whole article is arguing against.


## Which should you choose? Decision by scenario


Enough hedging; here is the explicit recommendation, framed as "choose X if" so you can self-select.


**Choose Warmly if:**


- You are standardized on HubSpot and want native, owned integration.
- You need proven, deep de-anonymization and mature intent orchestration.
- You value a large independent review base over a flat monthly price.


**Choose Knock AI if:**


- Your buyers scatter across Slack, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, and web chat.
- A predictable ~$1,000/mo line item beats modular quote-based pricing for you.
- You are comfortable underwriting an early-stage vendor on trajectory.


The second axis is team size and motion. Smaller, conversation-led teams tend to fit Knock AI; larger, HubSpot-centric, signal-led teams tend to fit Warmly; and demo-led teams should look at a different category entirely, including RepX.


If you cannot cleanly place yourself in one of those boxes, that is a signal in itself. It usually means visitor engagement is not your real bottleneck, and you should re-read the "when neither is right" section before you sign anything.


## A neutral scoring rubric (our methodology)


No top-ranking page applies a disclosed, repeatable rubric to *both* tools, so here is mine, scored 1 to 5 on six dimensions. The point is not the exact number, it is that you can see how I got there and disagree with a specific cell rather than the whole verdict.


Dimension Warmly Knock AI


Data quality / identification 5 3


Automation & orchestration depth 5 3


Pricing transparency 3 4


ICP fit breadth 4 4


Integration coverage 5 3


Review depth 5 2


**Total (out of 30)** **27** **19**


How I scored it: identification and orchestration reward Warmly's maturity; pricing transparency rewards Knock AI's flat line item; review depth punishes Knock AI's thin base, which is the honest cost of being early. If your weighting differs, for example if channel breadth is everything, recompute the cells, and if you want a fuller framework for this, my write-up on[how to compare GTM tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demostack-vs-walnut-a-comparison-of-its-features-and-pricing) walks through it. This rubric says Warmly is the safer default today, not that Knock AI is a bad bet for the right team.


Notice that Knock AI wins the one dimension buyers feel monthly, pricing transparency, and loses the ones they feel over a multi-year contract. That trade is the whole decision in miniature: a lower, clearer price now against proven depth and independent validation over time.


## How the HubSpot acquisition changes the Warmly decision


Every direct Warmly-vs-Knock comparison omits the most important 2026 development, which is that Warmly is now a HubSpot property. That single fact reshapes four things buyers should weigh before signing a multi-year deal.


First, roadmap: an acquired product's priorities bend toward the parent's platform, so expect Warmly's future to favor HubSpot-native workflows over neutral, best-of-breed flexibility. Second, pricing leverage: platform ownership changes packaging incentives over time, even if contracts hold steady in the near term.


Third, lock-in: native HubSpot integration is an advantage if you live in HubSpot and a risk if you might leave it. Fourth, and most concrete, is evaluation risk: this is exactly the kind of platform transition that makes a careful buyer pause and treat the change as a reason to re-examine the fit rather than a settled positive.


The neutral takeaway is to ask Warmly directly how packaging, data portability, and roadmap commitments will work under HubSpot, and to get the answers in writing. For a HubSpot-standardized team this acquisition is mostly upside; for a mixed-stack or HubSpot-skeptical team, it is the single strongest reason to shortlist Knock AI instead.


## When neither is right (honest alternatives)


Sometimes the correct answer is "different category," and a comparison that never says so is just a funnel. If your actual gap is not visitor engagement, do not force either tool into it.


- If you only need to identify companies, a visitor-ID-only tool is lighter and cheaper than either platform here.
- If your bottleneck is scheduling and hand-off, a meetings-first tool solves more than an engagement layer will.
- If your buyers convert by experiencing the product, a demo-led motion fits better, and you can even[automate your product demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-automation) so the demo itself does the qualifying.


Naming these honestly is the point of a neutral comparison: the tool that wins is the one matched to your bottleneck, not the one with the loudest page.


The failure mode I see most often is teams buying an engagement platform to fix a demand problem, then blaming the tool when traffic they never had fails to convert. Neither Warmly nor Knock AI manufactures intent; they act on it, so if the intent is not there yet, spend the budget upstream first.


## FAQ


**Can I use Warmly and Knock AI together?**


Technically yes, but it rarely makes sense to run two overlapping visitor-engagement platforms at once. You would pay twice for de-anonymization and risk conflicting routing, so pick the one whose motion fits and add adjacent tools only where they fill a real gap.


**Does Knock AI do visitor identification like Warmly?**


Yes, through its Knock Reveal component, though it is newer and less independently benchmarked than Warmly's de-anonymization. Warmly still carries the longer track record and the more widely cited coverage numbers, so demand a live accuracy test if identification is your core need.


**How long does it take to switch or implement either tool?**


Plan for weeks, not days, once routing, playbooks, and CRM sync are accounted for. The biggest time sink is usually untangling existing automations and record-creation logic, not learning the new interface.


**Which is better for SMB versus enterprise?**


Smaller, conversation-led teams often fit Knock AI's flat pricing and channel breadth, while larger, HubSpot-centric teams tend to fit Warmly's depth and native integration. Team motion matters more than headcount, so weight your buying pattern over your org chart.


**What changed after HubSpot bought Warmly?**


Warmly became a HubSpot property in 2026, which strengthens its native HubSpot integration but introduces roadmap, pricing, and lock-in questions. If you live in HubSpot it is largely upside; if you run a mixed stack, get roadmap and portability commitments in writing before you commit.
